co_upper_peanuts.blurb: Upper Peanuts is the higher of the two small Peanuts Walls above the western end of Eldorado Canyon, near Boulder. Thirteen routes, mostly traditional with a few bolted lines, run from one to four pitches. Grades cluster between 5.7 and 5.9, with a handful of harder 5.11 and 5.12 leads for strong climbers. The sandstone is lichen-covered and a little loose in places, so helmets make sense. The wall feels secluded compared with the busy canyon walls, and it looks out over the northern side of the canyon. Reaching it takes a talus scramble past the lower wall, so expect a longer, rougher walk than at the roadside crags.

co_wizard_rock.blurb: Wizard Rock is a single-pitch crag perched high on the south side of Boulder Canyon, just east of the Avalon cliffs, at roughly 7,500 feet. Thirteen routes of about 70 to 130 feet mix four bolted sport lines with gear climbs and a couple of top-rope options. Grades are friendly: mostly 5.7 to 5.9, a few easier lines, and a single 5.10 at the top end. It suits climbers who have ticked many canyon classics and want somewhere quieter. The base is reached by walking over from the large ledge above the Third Tier of Avalon, and descent is by lowering or a walk-off.

co_sport_land.blurb: Sport Land is Tonnere Tower's eastern side in Boulder Canyon, on the far bank of the creek opposite the Boulder Falls parking. It was bolted for moderate multi-pitch outings where a rack of quickdraws is enough, and most of its thirteen routes are sport climbs, mainly two pitches, with two trad lines mixed in. The grade spread centres on 5.10 and 5.11, with one or two easier and a couple of harder lines. The granite face catches the morning sun and goes into shade early in the afternoon, which makes it handy for hot summer days. Anchors are at the base of each route on a dirt ledge.
co_sport_land.parking_note: Park at the up-canyon end of the Boulder Falls pullout, about eight miles from town, or at the Boulder Slips pullout a little farther on.
co_sport_land.approach: Roughly 15 minutes. Get across Boulder Creek (a tyrolean in high water, wading or rock-hopping when it is low), then follow cairns through trees and talus and up a steep dirt path to the ledge below the routes.

co_subskull.blurb: Subskull is a sunny, windy, fairly secluded crag in Big Thompson Canyon near Estes Park, just down and left of Skull Rock. It is laid out in three parts: a slab on the left, a west-facing wall split by three cracks in the middle, and a south-facing wall with a low overhang on the right. Of its thirteen routes, about half are sport, the rest mostly trad plus one top-rope. Grades start near 5.8 and cluster around 5.9 to 5.11, topping out in the low 5.12s. Expect a walk of roughly half an hour on cairned trail.
co_subskull.parking_note: A large pullout with a memorial sits just downstream of mile marker 77 on US 34 in Big Thompson Canyon; the trail starts there.

co_southwest_face_finger_face.blurb: The Southwest Face, also called the Finger Face, is a less-than-vertical slab on North Gateway Rock in Garden of the Gods, Colorado Springs. It is named for a finger-shaped flake and sits south of the low-angle Tourist Gully ramp. The soft red sandstone holds thirteen routes, most of them bolted sport lines plus some trad and a top rope, and the grades are approachable: mostly 5.7 to 5.10, with one easy line and one 5.11. Protection is generally good, though hardware is old, so many climbers treat it as a place for steady moderates. Soft rock is easily damaged when wet.

co_fin_the_5.blurb: The Fin is the most eye-catching formation in the Jurassic Park cliffs above Lily Lake, south of Estes Park. It has a polished granite face with small edges that reward careful footwork. Most of the twelve routes are single-pitch sport lines, with four trad lines, running from 5.7 to the low 5.12s, and the middle grades of 5.9 to 5.12 hold most of them. Reaching the base is a steady uphill hike of about half an hour. Spring and fall tend to be the comfortable seasons, and mountain weather can turn quickly.

co_starcastle_the.blurb: The Starcastle is a crag in the Devil's Head area of the South Platte region, southwest of Denver, and it is the highest on the hill at around 9,500 feet, with tall turret-like formations. The climbing is steep, vertical face moves on defined edges, with some corners, small roofs and a few crack lines for trad gear. Twelve routes, eight sport and four trad, start at about 5.9 and run into the 5.12s, with most sitting in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, so it is better for experienced leaders than beginners. Reaching it means a faint trail from the overlook and a steep uphill push, finishing with a short fixed-rope downclimb to the first routes.
